content.text:
**One page is a good default—not a hard rule.** For most U.S. job applications, one or two pages is acceptable. ([case.edu](https://case.edu/studentlife/careercenter/career-development/career-resources/tips-job-seekers/resumes/resume-format?utm_source=openai))

- **If you’re a student or recent graduate:** aim for one page. ([bc.edu](https://www.bc.edu/bc-web/offices/studentaffairs/sites/careers/prepare/resume.html?utm_source=openai))
- **If you have substantial relevant experience:** two pages are fine; don’t cut strong accomplishments just to meet a one-page target. ([careerservices.fas.harvard.edu](https://careerservices.fas.harvard.edu/resources/gsas-masters-resume-cover-letter/?utm_source=openai))
- **Keep it readable:** don’t squeeze everything into tiny text or eliminate white space. Prioritize relevant content and clean formatting. ([cloudfront.careeronestop.org](https://cloudfront.careeronestop.org/Veterans/JobSearch/ResumesAndApplications/resume-overview.aspx?utm_source=openai))

My practical test: **Does page two add compelling evidence that you’re qualified, or just more history?** If it’s mostly older, unrelated jobs or repetitive duties, I’d trim it.

How many years of experience do you have, and what kind of role are you applying for?
